edges.note: Entrenchment of cisnormativity is offered as the reason self-protection dominates.
Author offers Peter's statements as grounds for classifying him as colluding.
Peter denies that language constrains or is forced on him.
Author offers John's statements as grounds for classifying him as colluding.
John says cisnormative language 'doesn't need fixing'.
Ashley says they 'never find out' whether race is the cause, against the Discussion's 'explicitly verbalized'.
Offered to explain why Samuel benefits from and does not notice cisnormativity.
The typology is the product of coding on shuster/Hollander themes.
'Identify discursive aggression' depends on shuster's definition.

anchors.exact: Strategies for Dealing with Cisnormative Discursive Aggression in the Workplace: Disruption, Criticism, Self-Enforcement, and Collusion

nodes.label: Title (author Miller): trans and gender-nonconforming workers deal with cisnormative discursive aggression through four strategies: disruption, criticism, self-enforcement and collusion.
nodes.short: Four workplace strategies against cisnormative aggression

anchors.exact: These discursive reactions include disruption, critique, self-enforcement, and collusion with cisnormative expectations.
These, it categorizes into four overlapping themes of response to discursive aggression: disruption, criticism, self-enforcement, and defensive collusion
Four main themes emerged in the form of strategies which were interpretable along a continuum of challenge/disruption and resignation/self-protection.

These reactions can be categorized as “disrupting,” “critiquing,” “self-enforcing,” and “colluding” and are rationalized through a scale ranging from challenge/disruption to self-protection/collusion.

nodes.label: Author: participants' reactions to workplace cisnormativity fall into a four-category typology (disrupting, critiquing, self-enforcing, colluding) arranged along a continuum from challenge to self-protection.
nodes.note: The author describes the categories as overlapping (b28) and states in the Limitations that the typology leans on categories already outlined by Hollander (2013) and shuster (2017).
nodes.short: Reactions form a four-category typology

anchors.exact: the overwhelming pervasiveness of cisnormativity—the assumption that being cisgender is natural and universal—in general discourse proves resistant to change and limits non-cisgender agency.
This resistance to change arises mainly from discursive enforcement in everyday contexts.
cisnormativity requires constant discursive work and the compliance of trans people to maintain the appearance of its naturalness
maintain cisnormativity constrains the agency of all but cisgender people and is primarily enforced through speech and language.

nodes.label: Author: cisnormativity remains pervasive, is maintained mainly through discursive enforcement in everyday speech, and constrains the agency of everyone who is not cisgender.
nodes.note: This is the theoretical premise the study starts from; the support offered is literature on gender as socially constructed plus an analogy from Coates's work on heteronormativity, not data from this study.
nodes.short: Cisnormativity is discursively enforced, constrains agency

anchors.exact: this framework provides greater clarity on the problem and then suggests avenues by which organizations and their management can better identify and act to remediate cisnormative oppression in the workplace.

This four-part typology of discursive strategies therefore can be useful in helping managers better identify and intervene upon problematic cisnormativity in the workplace that may otherwise have gone unnoticed, especially against trans women.

Managers who identify these patterns within their organizations would be encouraged to investigate and then shoulder the responsibilities of minimizing cisnormativity and transmisogyny in their departments and organizational cultures.

nodes.flag: The recommendation moves from describing how 18 interviewees respond to prescribing what managers should do (investigate, sensitivity training). No participant is reported to have proposed these measures, no intervention is observed or evaluated, and the added emphasis 'especially against trans women' is not tied to any comparison across groups in the data. Closing the gap would require evidence that managers using the typology detect or reduce cisnormativity.
nodes.label: Author: trans employees should not bear the burden of remediating cisnormativity; the typology can help managers identify it, and managers should take responsibility, including through trans- and gender-sensitivity training.
nodes.short: Managers should shoulder remediation, using typology
nodes.where: Introduction; Limitations, Practice Implications, and Conclusions

anchors.exact: Two participants, for whom the enforcement of binary concepts of gender is most explicit, actively resist and attempt to disrupt cisnormativity in the workplace.
For Mal and Ashley, their strategy of disrupting cisnormativity is socially costly and exhausting
They experience hostility and ostracism for their refusal to allow cisnormativity to be discursively constructed by others

nodes.label: Author: two participants (Mal and Ashley) actively disrupt cisnormativity at work and, as a result, experience hostility and ostracism, making the strategy socially costly and exhausting.
nodes.short: Disrupters face hostility and ostracism

anchors.exact: Ashley reported experiencing more direct confrontation than Mal. In this way, Ashley’s gender was more directly policed, and they believe this is because their co-workers, who are mostly white, feel more able to regulate and instruct a person of color.
with this being explicitly verbalized to Ashley because of their race.

nodes.flag: The Discussion says the racial motive was 'explicitly verbalized to Ashley', but Ashley's own quoted words (b41) say co-workers become 'defensive and evasive, so I never find out, but it's probably both'. The author's statement and the participant's account conflict; the attribution to race rests on Ashley's inference and a comparison of two people who differ in many other ways (workplace, style of intervention).
nodes.label: Author (endorsing Ashley's belief): Ashley's gender was more directly policed than Mal's because co-workers feel more able to regulate a person of color, and this racial motive was explicitly verbalized to Ashley.
nodes.short: Ashley policed more directly because of race

anchors.exact: Three more subjects were explicit about the ways in which cisnormativity is enforced in their workplace via discursive aggression and how difficult it makes their working lives. However, they reported only rarely raising the issue at work.

As a result, these subjects ultimately became exhausted and often engaged in self-enforcement (shuster, 2017) to avoid conflict. Moreover, all three voiced a fear of implicit or explicit professional repercussions if they fought workplace cisnormativity too vigorously
The three critics of cisnormativity address the problem explicitly but have become resigned and self-enforce most of the time

nodes.label: Author: three participants (Miranda, Iona, Tom) explicitly recognize and criticize workplace discursive aggression but rarely raise it at work, having become exhausted and fearful of professional repercussions, so they mostly self-enforce.
nodes.short: Critics recognize aggression but mostly self-enforce

anchors.exact: most subjects seemed unaware.

Holly, Stephen, and Dan accept dominant cisnormative language and assumptions as being normative, thus appropriate, and do so to the extent that they did not immediately recognize them as cisnormative.

Eleven subjects feel forced to self-enforce cisnormativity and discursive aggression to the extent that they are not consciously aware of its existence. However, when asked explicitly about certain discursive aggressions, they recognize their prevalence and acknowledge these to be burdensome.

nodes.flag: The classification treats participants' initial 'no pressure' answers as unawareness rather than as their own view. Recognition that the term applies came only after the interviewer clarified questions and explained the concept of 'discursive aggression' (b70, b73), and the quoted participants say things like 'Well, it's normal, isn't it?' and 'I don't really mind'. The claim that they 'feel forced' and find these 'burdensome' is not clearly voiced in the quotations; the alternative that they genuinely do not experience the language as aggression is not ruled out.
nodes.label: Author: eleven participants self-enforce cisnormativity to the point of not consciously recognizing it, accepting cisnormative language as normal, though when the concept is explained they acknowledge it applies and is burdensome.
nodes.short: Eleven self-enforce without conscious awareness

anchors.exact: an attitude of colluding with cisnormativity, far exceeding the mere acceptance of benefit exhibited by Samuel, presented in two of my subjects, though it manifested differently in each case.
This can only be explained in terms of a strategy of collusion with cisnormativity to deal with cisnormative discursive aggression.

He is well aware, in fact, that standing up for his identity and demanding equal status would have high social, thus professional, costs, and so he self-enforces cisnormativity, colludes, and perpetuates it while misdirecting his anger at those attempting to address the problem.
Peter’s overt hostility may indicate a form of self-protection through performing his masculinity in an aggressive, masculinist way

nodes.flag: The author states Peter's stance 'can only be explained' as a collusion strategy, yet both participants offer their own explanations (Peter: biological views; John: wanting acceptance as a colleague) that the author reinterprets as self-protection or fear. Nothing in the reported interviews rules out that they sincerely hold these views independent of any strategy for coping with aggression. The Discussion itself softens to 'may indicate' (b93).
nodes.label: Author: two participants (Peter and John) collude with cisnormativity — Peter through aggressive, essentialist masculinity as self-protection, John through fear of the ostracism that disrupters face — and this collusion is best explained as a strategy for dealing with discursive aggression.
nodes.short: Peter and John collude with cisnormativity

anchors.exact: Nope. No microaggressions and no need for safe spaces, trigger warnings, and diversity training.
Language is not violence. Nothing is forced on me. People talk in terms of male and female because this is how the species is perpetuated. It’s not a conspiracy.

nodes.flag: Peter directly rejects the author's premise that cisnormative language is a form of aggression that constrains trans people. The author treats his rejection as itself evidence of collusion; Peter treats it as a factual description of his workplace. The source records both without a way to adjudicate, and the reader should note the disagreement rather than assume either reading.
nodes.label: Peter (participant): he feels no pressure at work, language is not violence, nothing is forced on him, and people speak in male/female terms because that is how the species is perpetuated.
nodes.note: The author reports Peter cited evolutionary psychology sources in support; the source dismisses that literature but does not engage its content.
nodes.short: Peter: language is not violence

anchors.exact: Most people are straight, and most people are cis. This comes out in their language. It doesn’t need fixing. Besides, most people are really accommodating and give me very little problem. If you get in their faces, that will change. You’ll just make life harder for trans people.
It makes cis people wary of talking to trans people if they think they’re gonna be called out on their language every five minutes. We just want to be accepted as colleagues and friends.

nodes.flag: John's view conflicts with the author's position that cisnormative language needs remediation, while the author simultaneously concedes 'John's fears are not unfounded' (b87) and reports that the disrupters were indeed ostracized. The source thus supplies grounds for John's claim from its own data yet classifies his view as coerced collusion; the reader must weigh both readings.
nodes.label: John (participant): most people are cis and this shows in their language, which does not need fixing; confronting people over language makes cis people wary and makes life harder for trans people.
nodes.note: The author's own report that Mal and Ashley were ostracized (C5) bears on John's claim about the costs of confrontation, as the author acknowledges at b86–b87.
nodes.short: John: challenging language makes things worse

anchors.exact: It is significant that all 18 subjects identify cisnormativity and discursive aggression in their workplaces as outlined by shuster (2017) and Hollander (2013), but they differ widely in how they choose to address it.

nodes.flag: 'All 18 identify' sits uneasily with the Results, where eleven initially denied any pressure and Peter and John reject the framing outright; identification was reached only after the interviewer clarified questions or explained the scholarly term. What the participants themselves identified is that binary language is common, not necessarily that it is aggression.
nodes.label: Author: all 18 participants identify cisnormativity and discursive aggression in their workplaces, but differ widely in how they respond.
nodes.short: All eighteen identify workplace discursive aggression

anchors.exact: This was, by far, the most common response and comports with their need to communicate and interact within an epistemic system that does not include their experience
the need for self-protection considerably outweighs the fortitude needed to politically challenge discursive aggression and disrupt the dominant system.
acceptance and resignation proved the most common reactions, even despite significant expressions of anger and exhaustion.

nodes.flag: Frequency ('by far the most common') comes from an 18-person sample recruited by newspaper ad and snowball from two initial respondents in one city, yet the conclusion is phrased about cisnormativity 'throughout society and in the workplace'. The causal attribution — that resignation results from entrenchment and emotional labor rather than, say, participants' genuine indifference — rests on the author's interpretation of the self-enforcers (see C8).
nodes.label: Author: because cisnormativity is so entrenched and the emotional labor of resisting it so great, the need for self-protection outweighs the fortitude needed to challenge it, and acceptance and resignation were by far the most common reactions.
nodes.short: Self-protection outweighs challenge; resignation most common

anchors.exact: One significant limitation of this study was the relatively small sample size, which may have proven too small to have clearly derived this four-part typology for strategies used to endure and navigate workplace cisnormativity had those not been previously outlined in Hollander (2013) and developed by shuster (2017).

nodes.label: Author (limitation): the sample was small enough that the four-part typology might not have been clearly derived had the categories not already been outlined by Hollander (2013) and shuster (2017).
nodes.note: The author also recommends larger samples and inclusion of trans researchers in future work.
nodes.short: Small sample; typology leans on prior work

anchors.exact: Diamond and Butterworth (2008) demonstrate that gender, far from being fixed and stable, can vary considerably even within an individual’s lifetime.
Despite decades of scholarship showing that gender categories are neither stable nor natural

nodes.label: Cited scholarship (Foucault, Butler, West & Zimmerman, Diamond & Butterworth and others) holds that gender is socially constructed, performative and neither stable nor natural.
nodes.short: Literature: gender socially constructed, unstable

anchors.exact: Heterosexuality, like gender, is performed… in other words, sexual identity has to be repeatedly and interactionally achieved.

It follows that cisnormativity in gender identity is also repeatedly and interactionally achieved, and, indeed, language is permeated with cisnormative themes and tropes: “ladies and gentlemen,” “boys and girls,” “guys and girls,” “he or she,” “pregnant women,” etc.

nodes.label: The author extends Coates's account of heterosexuality as interactionally achieved through language to cisnormativity, listing everyday binary phrases as examples.
nodes.note: The move from heteronormativity to cisnormativity is argued by analogy ('It follows that'); the examples are illustrative phrases, not observed workplace data.
nodes.short: Analogy from heteronormativity to cisnormative language

anchors.exact: I’m not going to stay quiet when cis people try to impose their gender rules on me. It would make my life a lot easier if I did but why should I?
I will call out binary language when I hear it. It’s all over everyday speech, and the only way to change that is to challenge it every time.
Once, I listed twenty-six cis microaggressions I had experienced in a single week. Most people ignore my emails or just blandly thank me for raising the issues without addressing the issues!
I feel the one-to-one approach is harder to ignore, even if it gets me accused of creating a “hostile working environment,” as it has sometimes.

nodes.label: Mal and Ashley describe actively challenging binary language at work: refusing to stay quiet, calling out binary language, emailing lists of cis microaggressions to staff, and confronting individuals one-to-one.
nodes.short: Mal and Ashley describe disruptive practices

anchors.exact: People go to great lengths to avoid calling me anything at all just so they don’t have to say my pronouns.
There’s a real sense of entitlement that their convenience is more important than my reality.

They noted their manager has indicated that their confrontational nature makes the workplace a hostile environment on three separate occasions and asked them to “tone it down for the sake of the team.”
If I go to join in a conversation, people go quiet and then separate. No one asks me to go to lunch with them.
They just stop talking when I come into the room, and if I sit with someone at break and start conversation with them, I get one-word answers until I give up.

nodes.label: Mal and Ashley report co-workers avoiding their pronouns, resentment at being corrected, managerial warnings about a 'hostile environment', and social exclusion such as conversations stopping and being ignored at lunch or after work.
nodes.short: Mal and Ashley report resentment and ostracism

anchors.exact: Is it my gender or my race that makes you so determined not to listen to me? Sometimes I ask, but they just get more defensive and evasive, so I never find out, but it’s probably both

nodes.label: Ashley says white cis co-workers shut down when they raise gender and race, that they cannot find out whether gender or race is the cause, and that it is 'probably both'.
nodes.short: Ashley: cannot tell whether gender or race

anchors.exact: Because I’m tall and quite big-boned, I don’t “pass” [as a woman] and this makes people feel like they have the right to ask personal questions. I get patients who ask me “Are you a man?” or “Why are you wearing a skirt?”
[My manager] said she knows it’s hard but it’s part of the job.
[The nurse] said I need to think about it in the same way as mentally ill people.

nodes.label: Miranda describes patients asking whether she is a man, sarcastic misgendering, and a manager and nurse who frame this as ordinary job unpleasantness she should cope with.
nodes.short: Miranda: patient aggression, unsympathetic colleagues

anchors.exact: I get told how to be a woman properly by both cis men and cis women.
Men want to tell me how to be a man. They really think they’re helping.

nodes.label: Iona and Tom describe being misgendered on the phone and being 'taught' how to be a woman or a man by cis colleagues.
nodes.short: Iona and Tom: misgendering and gender coaching

anchors.exact: There’s no point with the little things. I feel like I’ve got to pick my battles and if I can’t get anyone to take explicit abuse seriously, they’re not going to care much about binary language.
say something, but people mostly mean well. I don’t want to ruin my working relationships.
I should speak up more. I used to, and I still do sometimes but I need to work with these guys and some of them are my friends.

nodes.label: Miranda, Iona and Tom explain why they rarely raise the issue: picking battles, not wanting to ruin working relationships, and needing to work with colleagues who are friends.
nodes.short: Critics' rationales for not speaking up

anchors.exact: But most of the interviewees eventually acquiesced to the power structure.

nodes.label: shuster (2017) reported the same pattern: interviewees who at first addressed mistakes eventually acquiesced to the power structure.
nodes.short: shuster found similar acquiescence

anchors.exact: Holly, a 54-year-old white trans woman, Stephen a 30-year-old black trans man, and Dan, a 24-year-old genderfluid white person all originally said “no” to being under any pressure to conform to gender norms, but this changed subsequent to clarifying my questions.
Well, it’s normal, isn’t it?
No, I’m not really under any pressure. No one tells me I shouldn’t present as a man or anything. They do assume I have a penis though.
I just think people understand better if you use the language they are used to.
Upon explaining the concept of “discursive aggression,” however, all three agreed that they can see how the term would apply.

nodes.label: Holly, Stephen and Dan initially said they felt no pressure to conform, then after clarification described binary language and genital assumptions as normal at work; after the term was explained, all three agreed it could apply.
nodes.short: Holly, Stephen, Dan: 'no pressure', then recognition

anchors.exact: No, it’s pretty cool. I’ve got a good team. They don’t really put pressure on me
but I don’t really mind. I think it’s meant in a kind of gender-neutral way.

nodes.label: Leah says the team is 'pretty cool' and applies no pressure, while also reporting being called 'guys', 'dude' and 'bro' and saying it is sometimes annoying but not really minded.
nodes.short: Leah: no pressure, but called 'dude'

anchors.exact: Samuel felt this cisnormativity and binary understanding of gender roles did not equate to discursive aggression because he is “a man on the floor,” that is, because he performs a masculine gender.

nodes.label: Samuel initially said gender was never discussed, then described 'girls in the office' and 'men on the floor' language, which he did not regard as aggression because he is 'a man on the floor'.
nodes.short: Samuel: binary language not aggression for him

anchors.exact: studies have shown trans men benefit from an elevation of status after transitioning (Dozier, 2005; Schilt, 2006)
While this was a relatively small group, the views of these men should be of particular concern for feminist and trans politics.

nodes.label: Cited studies (Dozier 2005; Schilt 2006; Abelson 2016) report that trans men gain status after transitioning and that a small group of young trans men hold anti-feminist attitudes.
nodes.short: Literature: trans men gain status

anchors.exact: He spoke over me repeatedly and redirected the conversation. He sat with legs spread taking up as much space as possible, spoke aggressively, and frequently leaned forward, as if to intimidate.
he responded scientistically by citing both popular and scholarly sources in evolutionary psychology

This performance of masculinity is toxic, actively colludes with cisnormativity, and its rise among trans men is alarming to social justice scholars working on issues affecting trans people (Abelson, 2016).

nodes.flag: The intimidation reading rests on one interviewer's interpretation of posture and tone in a single contentious interview, with no second observer, recording-based check, or participant validation reported. The author also notes the interview was contentious and that she did not share Peter's identity, so the reading may reflect the interaction as much as Peter's workplace strategy.
nodes.label: The author's own observations of Peter's interview conduct — speaking over her, posture and tone read as intimidation, citing evolutionary psychology — are offered as showing toxic, colluding masculinity.
nodes.short: Author's reading of Peter's demeanor

anchors.exact: His deflection from the problem and his accusation that it would cause hostility to address discursive aggression affecting trans people made it reasonable to infer that his anxiety was rooted in fear for his safety.
John’s fears are not unfounded.

nodes.label: The author infers from John's fearful tone and his blaming of those who challenge cisnormativity that his stance is rooted in fear for his safety and that he colludes to avoid social and professional costs.
nodes.note: The author concedes John's fears are 'not unfounded', which also bears on John's own claim (C11).
nodes.short: Author infers John's stance from fear

anchors.exact: Eleven people revealed countless
ways in which they self-enforced and maintained highly prevalent cisnormative cultures within their workplaces.

nodes.label: Eleven of the eighteen participants were classed as self-enforcing, making it the largest category.
nodes.short: Eleven of eighteen classed self-enforcing

anchors.exact: Of course, trans individuals cannot be expected to carry the burdens of disrupting cisnormativity in their workplaces or in culture more broadly
As trans people should not be considered to bear the twin responsibilities of being blamed for producing or having to overcome cisnormativity in the

nodes.label: The author argues that trans people cannot be expected to carry the burden of disrupting cisnormativity or be blamed for producing it, so institutional structures must be examined.
nodes.short: Burden should not fall on trans workers

anchors.exact: This study is based on in-depth, semi-structured interviews with eighteen individuals who identify as trans or gender nonconforming or who have a more fluid understanding of gender. They took place between February and August of 2017 in Ann Arbor, Michigan.
Seven self-identified as trans men, six as trans women, and five as non-binary or gender-fluid.
To recruit subjects, I placed a call in a small local newspaper and, having obtained two positive responses, used snowball sampling to recruit the remainder of the interviewees.
Semi-structured interviews of this sort tend to produce qualitative data with the least interviewer bias (although meaning-making is inevitably co-constituted by both parties).

because I wanted to draw out evidence of themes including self-enforcement and collusion, I often asked follow-up questions that inquired about their views of specific experience in light of existing scholarship of which they may not be aware

nodes.flag: The assertion that semi-structured interviews 'tend to produce qualitative data with the least interviewer bias' is given without a citation, and the author immediately describes follow-up questions intended to draw out specific themes and introducing scholarly terms participants may not know. The reader should treat responses that emerged after such prompting (especially in the self-enforcement category) as co-produced.
nodes.label: Eighteen in-depth semi-structured interviews (7 trans men, 6 trans women, 5 non-binary/gender-fluid) conducted Feb–Aug 2017 in Ann Arbor, recruited by a newspaper call plus snowball sampling, with open-ended questions and follow-ups designed to draw out self-enforcement and collusion themes, by a white cisgender bisexual interviewer.
nodes.note: The author discloses her positionality and states she tried to take a less assertive role.
nodes.short: Eighteen snowball-recruited semi-structured interviews

anchors.exact: Discursive aggression is “a term for the communicative acts used in social interaction to hold people accountable to social-and cultural-based expectations, and subsequently to reinforce inequality in everyday life” (shuster 2017, 483).

I then used selective thematic coding on the themes derived from shuster (2017) and Hollander (2013), while remaining open to additional themes, which were open-coded until theoretical saturation was recognized and themes were theorized into the present typology (Braun & Clarke, 2006).
Coding was performed by hand in a word processor on interview transcripts.

nodes.label: Transcripts were coded by hand by the author using selective thematic coding on themes taken from shuster (2017) and Hollander (2013), with open coding for additional themes until saturation; 'discursive aggression' is defined per shuster.
nodes.note: Self-enforcement and other-enforcement categories are taken from shuster; no second coder or inter-coder check is reported.
nodes.short: Single-author thematic coding using shuster's categories
